learn.hook: Atoms are like guests at a wedding: everyone who walks in must walk out — just with new partners!
points: A chemical reaction makes new substances. Signs: change in colour, change in state, gas given off, change in temperature or a precipitate forming.
A word equation names the reactants (left) and products (right), joined by an arrow: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide.
A skeletal equation uses formulae but may be unbalanced: Mg + O₂ → MgO.
Law of conservation of mass: mass is neither created nor destroyed, so each element must have the same number of atoms on both sides. We balance by changing coefficients, never the formulae.
State symbols show physical state: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water. Conditions such as heat or a catalyst are written above or below the arrow.

example.q: Balance: Fe + H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + H₂ (iron reacting with steam).
steps: Count atoms: left Fe 1, H 2, O 1; right Fe 3, H 2, O 4.
Start with the compound having the most atoms, Fe₃O₄: it has 4 O, so put 4 in front of H₂O.
Now left has 8 H, so put 4 in front of H₂.
Right has 3 Fe, so put 3 in front of Fe.
Check: Fe 3 = 3, H 8 = 8, O 4 = 4. Add states: steam is (g).

learn.reallife: When a Diwali sparkler (always lit with an adult around) glows bright white, metal powders such as aluminium or magnesium in it are reacting with oxygen — a real chemical change you can write as an equation.

games.title: Match the skeletal equation to its balanced form
Steps of balancing an equation
games.prompt: Put the steps in the order you do them
items: Write the skeletal equation with correct formulae
List the number of atoms of each element on both sides
Balance the compound with the most atoms first, using coefficients
Balance the remaining elements one by one
Re-count every element to check, then add state symbols

quiz.q: Why must a chemical equation be balanced?
options: Because mass is neither created nor destroyed in a reaction
To make the equation look neat
Because products must weigh more than reactants
To show the speed of the reaction
quiz.explain: The law of conservation of mass says total mass stays the same, so every atom present before the reaction must still be there after it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks balancing is only about appearance

quiz.q: Which of these is a correctly balanced equation?
quiz.explain: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO has 2 Mg and 2 O on each side.
quiz.mistake: Balances one element and forgets to re-check the other

quiz.q: In 3Fe + 4H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂, how many hydrogen atoms are on the left side?
quiz.explain: The coefficient 4 multiplies everything in H₂O, and each H₂O has 2 H atoms: 4 × 2 = 8.
quiz.mistake: Reads only the coefficient and ignores the subscript

quiz.q: While balancing, a student changes H₂O to H₂O₂ to get more oxygen. What is wrong?
options: Subscripts can be changed only for gases
It changes the substance itself; only coefficients may be changed
quiz.explain: H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, a different substance. Balancing is done by putting numbers in front of formulae, never by altering subscripts.
quiz.mistake: Believes subscripts can be adjusted like coefficients

quiz.q: What does the symbol (aq) mean in NaCl(aq)?
quiz.explain: (aq) stands for aqueous, meaning the substance is dissolved in water.
quiz.mistake: Confuses aqueous with liquid (l)

quiz.q: Which observation does NOT by itself show that a chemical reaction has happened?
options: A gas is given off when zinc is added to dilute acid
Blue copper sulphate solution turns pale green after an iron nail is dipped in it
A yellow precipitate forms when two solutions are mixed
Ice melting into water in a glass
quiz.explain: Melting ice is only a change of state of the same substance (water); no new substance forms.
quiz.mistake: Treats every change of state as a chemical change

quiz.q: In 2Pb(NO₃)₂ → 2PbO + 4NO₂ + O₂, how many oxygen atoms are there on the right side?
quiz.explain: 2PbO gives 2, 4NO₂ gives 8 and O₂ gives 2, so 2 + 8 + 2 = 12 — the same as 2 × 6 = 12 on the left.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by the coefficients

quiz.q: Which balanced equation correctly shows aluminium burning in oxygen?
quiz.explain: 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃ has 4 Al and 6 O on each side.
quiz.mistake: Balances aluminium but leaves oxygen unequal

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: 'Why can't I just change H₂O into H₂O₂ to balance my equation? Explain balancing to me!'
teach.praise: Chirp! Same atoms on both sides, fixed with coefficients — mass is saved!
teach.nudge: Good start! But what do we change to balance — the formula or the number in front? And why?

learn.hook: Some reactions join things, some break them apart, and some are like a dance where partners swap!
points: Combination: two or more reactants form one product, e.g. CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ (quicklime to slaked lime, with lots of heat).
Decomposition: one reactant breaks into simpler products using heat (thermal), light (photolytic) or electricity (electrolytic), e.g. CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ on heating.
Displacement: a more reactive element pushes a less reactive one out of its compound, e.g. Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu.
Double displacement: two compounds exchange ions; often an insoluble precipitate forms, e.g. Na₂SO₄ + BaCl₂ → BaSO₄↓ (white) + 2NaCl.
Exothermic reactions release heat (burning, respiration); endothermic reactions absorb energy (most decompositions, photosynthesis).

example.q: Think it through: an iron nail is dipped in blue copper sulphate solution for 20 minutes. What do you see, and what type of reaction is it?
steps: Iron is more reactive than copper.
So iron displaces copper from copper sulphate: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu.
Copper deposits on the nail as a brownish coat.
Iron sulphate solution is pale green, so the blue colour fades.
One element replaces another in a compound — a displacement reaction.
example.answer: The nail turns brownish and the blue solution fades towards pale green: a displacement reaction.

learn.reallife: Whitewashing walls before festivals uses slaked lime. It slowly reacts with carbon dioxide in air to form a thin layer of calcium carbonate, which gives walls a shine after two or three days.

games.title: Reaction type check
items: Respiration is an exothermic reaction.
Glucose combines with oxygen in our cells and releases energy.
When water is electrolysed, the volume of hydrogen collected is double the volume of oxygen.
Water is H₂O, so 2 volumes of hydrogen form for every 1 volume of oxygen.
Heating ferrous sulphate crystals is a combination reaction.
It breaks one compound into Fe₂O₃, SO₂ and SO₃ — a thermal decomposition.
Mixing lead nitrate and potassium iodide solutions gives a yellow precipitate of lead iodide.
Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2KI → PbI₂ (yellow) + 2KNO₃, a double displacement reaction.
Copper can displace iron from iron sulphate solution.
Copper is less reactive than iron, so no displacement happens.
Most decomposition reactions need energy in the form of heat, light or electricity.
Breaking a compound apart needs energy, so these reactions are usually endothermic.

quiz.q: Quicklime reacts vigorously with water, releasing a lot of heat. Which type of reaction is this?
quiz.explain: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ joins two reactants into one product and gives out heat.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up 'joining' with 'breaking' and heat given with heat taken

quiz.q: Heating lead nitrate gives off brown fumes. What are these fumes?
quiz.explain: 2Pb(NO₃)₂ → 2PbO + 4NO₂ + O₂. Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) is the brown gas; oxygen is colourless.
quiz.mistake: Thinks oxygen is coloured

quiz.q: White silver chloride turns grey in sunlight. What type of reaction is this?
quiz.explain: Light splits silver chloride into silver and chlorine: 2AgCl → 2Ag + Cl₂. This idea was used in black-and-white photography.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the energy source (light) to the type of decomposition

quiz.q: Which is a double displacement reaction?
quiz.explain: Here the two compounds swap ions: sodium joins chloride and barium joins sulphate. BaSO₄ forms a white precipitate.
quiz.mistake: Confuses single displacement (element + compound) with double displacement

quiz.q: Why does a white solid form when sodium sulphate and barium chloride solutions are mixed?
options: Barium sulphate formed is insoluble in water
quiz.explain: A precipitate is an insoluble product. Barium sulphate does not dissolve, so it appears as a white solid; sodium chloride stays dissolved.
quiz.mistake: Thinks common salt is the precipitate

quiz.q: Which of these is an endothermic process?
options: Decomposition of calcium carbonate into lime
quiz.explain: Calcium carbonate must be heated strongly to break into CaO and CO₂, so it absorbs heat.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every reaction gives out heat

quiz.q: Zinc granules are added to dilute sulphuric acid. Which gas is released?
quiz.explain: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂. Zinc displaces hydrogen from the acid.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a gas from the acid's formula without thinking of displacement

quiz.q: In the electrolysis of water, which gas collects at the electrode where the volume is larger?
quiz.explain: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂, so hydrogen's volume is twice that of oxygen.
quiz.mistake: Thinks oxygen is produced in larger amount because water 'contains' oxygen

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'Iron nail plus blue liquid made the nail brown! Which type of reaction is that, and how is it different from combination?'
teach.praise: Tweet-tweet! The more reactive iron kicked copper out — displacement! And I know combination joins things.
teach.nudge: Nearly! Why can iron push copper out but copper cannot push iron out?

learn.hook: Every time something gains oxygen, something else is losing it — oxidation and reduction always come as a pair!
points: Oxidation: a substance gains oxygen or loses hydrogen. Reduction: a substance loses oxygen or gains hydrogen.
When both happen in the same reaction it is a redox reaction, e.g. CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O (CuO is reduced, H₂ is oxidised).
Heating copper powder in air: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO. The brown surface turns black as copper is oxidised.
Corrosion: a metal is slowly attacked by air, moisture or acids. Iron rusts (reddish-brown), silver turns black and copper gets a green coat.
Rancidity: fats and oils in food get oxidised, changing smell and taste. Airtight containers, antioxidants and filling chip packets with nitrogen slow it down.

example.q: Think it through: in ZnO + C → Zn + CO, which substance is oxidised and which is reduced?
steps: Zinc oxide (ZnO) loses its oxygen and becomes Zn — loss of oxygen is reduction.
Carbon (C) gains oxygen and becomes CO — gain of oxygen is oxidation.
Both happen together, so this is a redox reaction.
example.answer: ZnO is reduced and C is oxidised; it is a redox reaction.

learn.reallife: Chip packets puff up because they are filled with nitrogen instead of air, so the oil in the chips does not get oxidised and turn rancid.

items.text: In CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, copper oxide is ___.
Food packets are flushed with ___ gas to prevent rancidity.
Silver articles turn black in air because a coating of silver ___ forms.

items.q: Oxidation of fats and oils in food?

quiz.q: In CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, which substance is oxidised?
quiz.explain: Hydrogen gains oxygen to become water, so hydrogen is oxidised. Copper oxide loses oxygen and is reduced.
quiz.mistake: Picks the substance that contains oxygen at the start as the one oxidised

quiz.q: Brown copper powder is heated in a china dish in air. What does it turn into?
quiz.explain: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO. Copper gains oxygen and the surface becomes black copper(II) oxide.
quiz.mistake: Confuses heating in air with slow corrosion that gives a green coat

quiz.q: In MnO₂ + 4HCl → MnCl₂ + 2H₂O + Cl₂, what happens to HCl?
options: It is oxidised because it loses hydrogen
It is reduced because it gains oxygen
It is neither oxidised nor reduced
It is reduced because it loses chlorine
quiz.explain: HCl loses hydrogen to become Cl₂; loss of hydrogen is oxidation. MnO₂ loses oxygen, so it is reduced.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that oxidation can also mean loss of hydrogen

quiz.q: Which two things are needed for iron to rust?
quiz.explain: Iron rusts only when both air (oxygen) and moisture are present. Without either one, rusting stops.
quiz.mistake: Thinks water alone or air alone is enough

quiz.q: Why do chips makers fill packets with nitrogen?
options: To make the chips crispier by heating
To kill insects by poisoning them
To keep oxygen away so the oil does not turn rancid
quiz.explain: Nitrogen is unreactive. Replacing air with it keeps oxygen away, slowing oxidation of fats and oils.
quiz.mistake: Does not link rancidity with oxidation by oxygen

quiz.q: A copper vessel left in moist air for months gets a green coating. This is an example of —
quiz.explain: Copper reacts slowly with moist carbon dioxide in air, forming a green basic copper carbonate layer — corrosion.
quiz.mistake: Uses rancidity for metals instead of food

quiz.q: In ZnO + C → Zn + CO, the substance reduced is —
quiz.explain: Zinc oxide loses oxygen to form zinc, so ZnO is reduced.
quiz.mistake: Marks the product instead of the reactant that lost oxygen

quiz.q: Which statement about a redox reaction is correct?
options: Oxidation and reduction take place together
No electrons or atoms change partners
quiz.explain: If one substance gains oxygen, another must lose it in the same reaction, so oxidation and reduction occur together.
quiz.mistake: Thinks oxidation and reduction are separate reactions

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'Mummy's namkeen tastes funny after a month open. Is that the same oxidation as iron rusting? What is oxidation anyway?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Gaining oxygen spoils oil (rancidity) and eats metal (corrosion) — clever!
teach.nudge: Good! But what exactly is gained in oxidation? And what do we call it when it happens to food oils?
